clue.text: On postcard, she composed phrase describing America

indicators.note: something composed has been put together anew, so these words are rearranged into fresh order

parts.note: the thirteen letters of these three words, taken together

explanation.surface: A woman writes a postcard and coins a phrase about America while she is at it.
explanation.walkthrough: The pond is the Atlantic, so from Britain the United States lies ACROSS THE POND.
explanation.definitionFit: British speakers use this idiom for the USA, which lies over the Atlantic Ocean from them.

clue.text: Shorten to make tight and fashionable

parts.note: close can mean tight, as in a close fit
in is a common word for in fashion

explanation.surface: A tailor's instruction: take a garment in so it fits snugly and looks stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: The tailoring surface suggests taking clothes in, but the definition is about days growing shorter.
explanation.definitionFit: When autumn days close in, daylight hours grow fewer, so the phrasal verb means become shorter.

clue.text: Restricted, slim fit of pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so a pants version of these letters is a botched, jumbled one

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: A description of tight-fitting trousers, cut close to restrict movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants reads as trousers in the surface; here it is British slang meaning rubbish or poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Places that are off-limits are out of bounds, with entry forbidden or restricted to most people.

clue.text: 'Insatiety' describes creative Frenchman

indicators.note: to describe is literally to draw a line around, so the outer word encloses what we want

parts.note: the letters run inside this word, after its first two

explanation.surface: A word meaning greed that cannot be satisfied seems to characterise some artistic French figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Erik SATIE was a French composer, author of the Gymnopédies.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer Erik Satie was French and an innovative artist, so creative Frenchman fits by example.

clue.text: Photos identifying leaders: 'laughable tosh'

parts.note: heads are leaders, as of departments or schools

indicators.note: something laughable is a joke, a mess, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses as nonsense the claim that some pictures reveal who is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Headshots are portrait photographs of the face, as used by actors and on official passes.

clue.text: Boat capsized in still waters

indicators.note: a capsized vessel is upside down, and in a down entry that turns the word bottom to top

parts.note: a sloop is a single-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: A boat turns over on a calm lake or pond.
explanation.definitionFit: Pools are small bodies of standing water, so still waters is a fair plural paraphrase.

clue.text: Ant scrambled up mountain without man's involvement

indicators.note: scrambled means mixed up, so the three letters of that insect are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Urals are a Russian mountain range; a Ural is one of them

explanation.surface: An ant clambers up a mountainside in the wild, far from humans.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, up places the first piece on top of the mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something natural arises from nature itself, not made or influenced by human hands.

clue.text: With trendy element, weakens story

indicators.note: with here means having inside, so the phrase for weakens contains the trendy part

parts.note: waters down means dilutes or weakens
hip means trendy, an element added within

explanation.surface: Adding something fashionable dilutes a narrative.
explanation.walkthrough: Element hints at a component placed inside; the story is Richard Adams's 1972 novel about rabbits.
explanation.definitionFit: Watership Down is a famous 1972 novel by Richard Adams, so a story by example.

clue.text: Not working until The Telegraph's approaching deadline

parts.note: a system that is down is not working
to can mean until, as in nine to five
taken as written
a wire is a telegraph message; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A newspaper's staff are idle until the paper nears its press deadline.
explanation.walkthrough: The Telegraph is a British newspaper in the surface, but here simply a telegram or wire.
explanation.definitionFit: Going down to the wire means lasting until the last possible moment, as a deadline approaches.

clue.text: Unpleasantly cold, a roly-poly pudding

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: roly-poly suggests rolling over, so the dessert word is turned back to front

parts.note: a fool is a fruit and cream dessert

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a jam roly-poly pudding has been served unpleasantly cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Jam roly-poly is a British rolled suet pudding; here roly-poly just means rolled over. A fool is a British fruit-and-cream dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: An aloof person is distant and chilly in manner, cold in a way others find off-putting.

clue.text: Musical number requiring tenor with nifty footwear

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tenor

indicators.note: nifty means deft and clever, as with nimble moves that rearrange the letters

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A song-and-dance routine needs a tenor wearing smart tap shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea for Two is a famous song from the 1925 musical No, No, Nanette.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea for Two is a well-known song from a stage show, so a musical number by example.

clue.text: Kohl has row in Europe, the old rivals taking sides

definitions.note: singular, while the answer is plural

indicators.note: in places the row inside the string of letters that follows

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for Europe
ye is an archaic form of the
a row is a line

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its two edges, so only its outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of rivals

explanation.surface: Helmut Kohl, German chancellor, quarrels in Europe with the old rivals choosing which side to back.
explanation.walkthrough: Kohl is the German chancellor in the surface, but kohl is also black eye make-up. LINE sits inside E-YE-RS.
explanation.definitionFit: Kohl is a dark cosmetic powder applied around the eyes, a kind of eyeliner.

clue.text: Samson gutted, full of anger: 'Delilah!'

indicators.note: full of means holding something inside, so the anger word goes between the remaining letters
gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters of the name

parts.note: the first and last letters of Samson
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Samson, devastated and furious, cries out the name of the woman who betrayed him.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible Delilah lured Samson to his downfall by cutting his hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Delilah is the archetypal temptress, and a siren is a seductive woman who lures men to ruin.

clue.text: Nosing around, taking in north Berkshire village

indicators.note: taking in means absorbing, so an extra letter goes inside
around suggests turning about, so the letters of the sniffing word are spun into new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Someone snoops around the countryside, visiting a village in the north of Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county west of London; Sonning is a Thames-side village there.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonning is a small village on the River Thames in the English county of Berkshire.

clue.text: Ignore Brexiteer admitting defeat before start of referendum

indicators.note: before places one piece ahead of the next in the answer
admitting means letting in, so the politician's name takes another word inside

parts.note: Michael Gove, a leading Conservative campaigner for Brexit
a defeat is a loss

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the first letter of referendum

explanation.surface: A Leave campaigner concedes the referendum was lost, even before it began.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Gove is a British Conservative politician who campaigned to leave the EU in 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: To gloss over a problem is to pass over it quickly, treating it as unimportant: deliberately disregard it.

clue.text: Play a game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor of Venice
second meaning: a board game with black and white discs, also called Reversi

explanation.walkthrough: Play looks like a verb inviting a game; it is a noun for a stage drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names both a Shakespeare tragedy and a two-player board game of flipping counters.

clue.text: Bring her a sinister omen

indicators.note: sinister means crooked or wrong, so these letters are twisted out of their order

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: Someone delivers a woman an ill-boding portent.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbinger is a forerunner or sign of what is to come, much like a portent.

clue.text: One's in independent company, producing French playwright

indicators.note: in places the first phrase inside the letters that follow it

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for independent
one's written without its apostrophe
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Someone belongs to a small independent theatre company that is staging a French dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: One's, apostrophe ignored, is the inserted piece; the outer letters are two standard abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugène Ionesco was a Romanian-born dramatist who wrote in French, a pioneer of the Theatre of the Absurd.

clue.text: City's 'New Look, Old Vibe' essentially retrograde

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
an air is a look or manner
O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so those middle letters are read in reverse
the essence of a word is its core, so only its middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of vibe

explanation.surface: A city is described as having a fresh look but an old-fashioned, backward-looking atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is Kenya's capital and largest urban centre in East Africa.

clue.text: Holy man threw up: blimey

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for saint

indicators.note: up here means in disorder, as when things are churned up

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A saint vomited, and an onlooker exclaims in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Threw up suggests being sick; up instead signals the jumbling. Blimey is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Strewth is an Australian and British exclamation of surprise or dismay, equivalent to that other interjection.

clue.text: With tweaks, could be an award-winning actress

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
to tweak is to alter slightly

explanation.surface: A small adjustment might turn someone into a prize-winning performer.
explanation.walkthrough: Julie Walters is a British actress who has won BAFTAs and an Olivier award; could be marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to Julie Walters, a much-honoured British stage and screen performer.

clue.text: Impersonating wild dingo

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the dog's letters run loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone does an impression of an Australian wild dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing someone, informally, means mimicking them, as when a comedian performs an impression.

clue.text: Leave to become less popular

definitions.meaning: first meaning: depart, exit a place
second meaning: fall from fashion, as styles do

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one instruction, it sounds like quitting in order to lose popularity; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both exit a room and fall out of fashion, as fads eventually do.

clue.text: Full of wickedness, Lawson's cooking for family

indicators.note: full of means holding inside, so the wrongdoing word is enclosed
cooking means mixing up ingredients, so the surname's letters are stirred into new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
sin is wickedness

explanation.surface: Nigella Lawson, the TV cook, makes something wickedly indulgent for her family.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigella Lawson is a British television cook known for indulgent recipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sons-in-law are relatives by marriage, members of the wider family.

clue.text: Coronary artery bypasses? No!

indicators.note: a bypass runs through a stretch, so the answer passes across the join of the two words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone asks if heart surgery is needed and gets a firm refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: Nary a is dialect for not a single one.
explanation.definitionFit: Nary a means not one, an emphatic negative, as in nary a word was spoken.

clue.text: No matter which of you hoovers, we will be messy

indicators.note: a messy result is disordered, so these letters end up in a jumbled order

parts.note: the letters of these two words together

explanation.surface: A housemate warns that whoever does the vacuuming, the place will still be untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: To hoover is British for to vacuum-clean, from the brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: Whosoever means any person at all, whoever it may be, so no matter which individual.

clue.text: Feminist with endless desire, foremost of radicals

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: greed is excessive desire

indicators.note: foremost is the very front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of radicals

explanation.surface: A campaigner for women's rights, driven by limitless ambition, leads the radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: Germaine Greer is the Australian author of The Female Eunuch.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine Greer is a celebrated feminist writer and academic, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: In part of Australia, to interbreed is epitome of bravery

parts.note: Victoria is an Australian state
to cross animals or plants is to interbreed them

explanation.surface: In some Australian region, crossbreeding livestock is held up as the height of courage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Victoria Cross is the highest British and Commonwealth military award for gallantry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victoria Cross is the supreme military decoration for valour, so it embodies courage.
